bib.title: Self-collaboration Code Generation via ChatGPT
bib.venue: ACM Trans. Softw. Eng. Methodol. (arXiv v3, 11 May 2024)

question: Can several instances of one LLM, given role instructions in a software-development workflow (analyst, coder, tester), solve code-generation tasks better than a single LLM agent?
hypothesis: Role-playing LLM agents organised by a software-development methodology (waterfall) and exchanging natural-language feedback outperform a single agent, without training or human intervention.
contributions: A self-collaboration framework with role instructions letting LLM agents collaborate to generate code for complex requirements.
An elementary team of analyst, coder and tester following a simplified waterfall model.
Significant gains over a single LLM agent (ChatGPT, GPT-3.5) on multiple code-generation benchmarks.
Notable effectiveness on more complex real-world, repository-level style tasks that a single agent struggles with (case studies).

method.summary: Three ChatGPT sessions are initialised once with role instructions (team description, role description, user requirement) as analyst, coder and tester. They exchange natural-language outputs through a shared blackboard: analyst writes decomposition and plan, coder writes code, tester simulates testing (no execution) and writes a report, coder repairs, until tester says 'Code Test Passed' or max interaction n is reached. Nothing is trained.
method.task: Python code generation from natural-language requirements (function-level and small projects)

datasets.name: MBPP (sanitized)
datasets.preprocessing: each task: NL description, code solution, 3 test cases

datasets.name: MBPP-ET and HumanEval-ET

datasets.size: first 1000 tasks from interview and competition levels

models.name: Fastchat-3B, ChatGLM-6B, MPT-7B, Vicuna-7B/13B, HuggingChat-30B, Dromedary-65B

other.note: AlphaCode and PaLM Coder numbers copied from original papers; others rerun under same settings

inference.samples: one generation per task (top-1); seeds and repeat runs not stated
inference.prompting: Role instruction given once per agent at initialisation: team description + role description + user requirement. Roles interact in NL via a blackboard; output y updated only at coding stage. JSON output recommended for multi-component outputs. Default setting for most experiments is NL-only; Table 1 uses NL + signature + use cases.

parameters.roles: analyst, coder, tester (also tested: +compiler team, driver+observer pair programming)
parameters.end_condition: max interaction n reached or tester confirms no issues
parameters.tester: simulates testing with the model, does not execute code (compiler variant uses HumanEval use cases as public tests)
parameters.iter_improving_baseline: instruction 'Please improve this code', max 10 iterations

other.limit: max tokens 512 and ChatGPT token limit restricted MI exploration to 1 to 4

metrics.name: Pass@1
metrics.definition: unbiased Pass@1 (Chen et al.): expectation over problems of indicator that top-1 generated code passes all test cases

baselines: Code LLMs (AlphaCode, Incoder, CodeGeeX, StarCoder, CodeGen, PaLM Coder, CodeLlama, CodeX, CodeX+CodeT)
eval.protocol: Single deterministic run per setting (temperature 0); no seeds, variance or significance tests reported. Role ablations, alternative teams (compiler, pair programming) and non-role-playing baselines (zero-shot instruction, 4-shot) on HumanEval/MBPP; manual error analysis on HumanEval; token cost normalised to coder=1.

availability.data: public benchmarks; role instructions in Fig 3 and appendix

prompts.text: I want you to act as a developer on our development team. You will receive plans from a requirements analyst or test reports from a tester. Your job is split into two parts: 1. If you receive a plan from a requirements analyst, write code in Python that meets the requirements following the plan. Ensure that the code you write is efficient, readable, and follows best practices. 2. If you receive a test report from a tester, fix or improve the code based on the content of the report. Ensure that any changes made to the code do not introduce new bugs or negatively impact the performance of the code. Remember, do not need to explain the code you wrote.
prompts.where: Fig 3 (team description prefix: 'There is a development team that includes a requirements analyst, a developer, and a quality assurance tester.')

prompts.text: 1. Decompose the requirement into several easy-to-solve subproblems that can be more easily implemented by the developer. 2. Develop a high-level plan that outlines the major steps of the program. Remember, your plan should be high-level and focused on guiding the developer in writing code, rather than providing implementation details.

1. Test the functionality of the code to ensure it satisfies the requirements. 2. Write reports on any issues or bugs you encounter. 3. If the code or the revised code has passed your tests, write a conclusion "Code Test Passed". Remember, the report should be as concise as possible, without sacrificing clarity and completeness of information. Do not include any error handling or exception handling suggestions in your report.

There is a pair programming team that includes a driver, and an observer. The team needs to develop a program that meets a requirement. The different roles have different divisions of labor and need to cooperate with each others.
prompts.where: Appendix E (driver and observer instructions also given there)

limits: Benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CoderEval) are function-level and differ from real software development; repository-level claims rest on two qualitative case studies (authors concede, Sec 6).
Tester simulates testing with the LLM without executing code; no ground-truth execution feedback in the main team.
Single run at temperature 0; no seeds, variance or significance tests.
Authors suspect data contamination in MBPP (App C); analyst role hurts on NL-only MBPP.
Gains need capable base models: self-collaboration emerges around 7B parameters and depends on domain expertise, instruction following and reasoning (Sec 4.4).
Team structure may need adjustment per problem; small human guidance suggested.
Cost: more tokens than a single coder (Fig 7, values only in figure); ChatGPT token limits capped interactions at 4.
Baselines: self-planning and self-debugging were run with prompts from original papers; CoT noted as unsuited to code.
Dated: ChatGPT gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 and 2023-era baselines; the multi-agent field (e.g. later frameworks) postdates this.
